problem_stated.one_line: Pre-trained LMs hold factual knowledge implicitly in their parameters, but that store cannot be expanded, revised, or inspected; the paper proposes to attach an explicit, human-readable, replaceable text index to a pre-trained seq2seq generator and fine-tune the pair end-to-end for knowledge-intensive generation, not just extraction.

verbatim_anchors.quote: their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and hence on knowledge-intensive tasks, their performance lags behind task-specific architectures. Additionally, providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems.
They cannot easily expand or revise their memory, can't straightforwardly provide insight into their predictions, and may produce “hallucinations”
Pre-trained models with a differentiable access mechanism to explicit non-parametric memory have so far been only investigated for extractive downstream tasks.

REALM [20] and ORQA [31], two recently introduced models that combine masked language models [8] with a differentiable retriever, have shown promising results, but have only explored open-domain extractive question answering. Here, we bring hybrid parametric and non-parametric memory to the “workhorse of NLP,” i.e. sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models.

problem_stated.framing_metaphor: Parametric memory (the generator's weights) vs non-parametric memory (a dense vector index of Wikipedia). The paper explicitly names both: 'We refer to the document index as the non-parametric memory' [rag Sec.2.2, line 231] and 'We refer to the BART generator parameters theta as the parametric memory henceforth' [rag Sec.2.3, line 241]. NOTE for the monograph: STC-STYLE-NOTATION Sec.2.4 forbids the parametric/non-parametric dichotomy as imprecise; render them as Theta and E respectively.
problem_stated.what_it_is_NOT_about: The paper contains no notion of idle time, offline pre-computation per context, budget amortization, consolidation, sleep, forgetting, or model-authored memory writes. Searching the vendored text for 'sleep', 'consolidat', 'offline', 'amortiz', 'idle' returns nothing. RAG is the E-path's READ machinery, five years before the sleep-time framing existed.

inherited_open_question.detail: The paper never quotes an open question from a named predecessor. It states a *scope gap* in prior work and fills it. The closest thing to an inherited question is the observation that the differentiable-retriever line had only been applied to extraction: 'REALM [20] and ORQA [31] ... have shown promising results, but have only explored open-domain extractive question answering' [rag Sec.1, lines 41-43 / 116-117]. That is the authors' characterization of REALM/ORQA, not a question REALM or ORQA posed.

second_anchor.quote: There has been extensive previous work proposing architectures to enrich systems with non-parametric memory which are trained from scratch for specific tasks, e.g. memory networks [64, 55], stack-augmented networks [25] and memory layers [30]. In contrast, we explore a setting where both parametric and non-parametric memory components are pre-trained and pre-loaded with extensive knowledge.
second_anchor.reading: The second gap is 'trained from scratch per task' vs 'pre-trained and reusable'. Again a gap the authors assert, not a question they were handed.

what_it_implicitly_answers: How does one make E a first-class read path that a *generator* (not an extractor) can condition on, and train the read path by task loss alone with no supervision over which document is correct? Answer: treat z as a latent variable and marginalize over top-K [rag Sec.2.1, Sec.2.4].

Can an external store substitute for parameters? The paper answers with a parameter-count argument: 626M trainable parameters beat T5-11B on NQ (44.5 vs 34.5) and T5-large 770M scores 28.9 EM [rag App. G, lines 1423-1427; Table 1].

Can world knowledge be updated without touching Theta? Answer: replace the index. 'we demonstrate that the non-parametric memory can be replaced to update the models' knowledge as the world changes' [rag Sec.1, line 143; Sec.4.5 index hot-swapping, lines 627-796]. THIS is the sentence the whole E-path descends from.
inherited_open_question.monograph_finding: The un-inherited question is itself the finding. RAG originates in the IR/open-domain-QA community and inherits nothing from the continual-learning or fast-weight communities. Its bibliography confirms this (see cross_path_citations). The E-path therefore does not begin as an answer to a memory-consolidation question; it begins as an answer to an information-retrieval question, and only later gets re-read as a memory architecture. The bridge-in for the E-path chapter cannot be a quoted predecessor question - it must be the assertion of a scope gap in REALM/ORQA plus the index-hot-swap demonstration.

core_mechanism.summary_one_line: Read-only E-path: E is a frozen dense index of 21M Wikipedia text chunks; ret(E,q) is a top-K MIPS lookup whose scores are a learned distribution over latent documents, and equation (R) is realized by marginalizing the generator's output over those K documents either once per sequence or once per token.

Cite them by section and position, e.g. '[rag Sec.2.1, RAG-Sequence display]', '[rag Sec.2.2, retriever display]'. The instruction to cite 'original equation number' cannot be honoured because none exist; the convention below is the substitute and must be used consistently in the chapter.

state_decomposition.Theta: Two learnable blocks, both slow weights in the unified sense: (i) the generator parameters, BART-large, called theta in the paper - 400M [rag Sec.2.3, line 237] / 406M [rag App. G, line 1376]; (ii) the query encoder BERT_q, BERT-BASE, 110M [rag App. G, line 1375]. Both move only in the fine-tuning outer loop.
state_decomposition.Theta_frozen: The document encoder BERT_d, BERT-BASE, 110M, is NOT trained: 'we ... keep the document encoder (and index) fixed, only fine-tuning the query encoder BERT_q and the BART generator' [rag Sec.2.4, lines 254-255]. It is used once, offline, to build E.
state_decomposition.W: EMPTY. RAG has no fast weights. Nothing in the model changes state within or across a query. The KV cache of the generator is ordinary decoding scratch, not a W in the (U-W) sense. This is the cleanest instance in the corpus of a paper that touches Theta and E and leaves W untouched.
state_decomposition.E: A dense vector index over 21M documents: one December 2018 Wikipedia dump, each article split into disjoint 100-word chunks [rag Sec.3, lines 280-283]. Physically 21M vectors of 728 dimensions = 15.3B values, storable at 8-bit [rag App. G, lines 1427-1429], held in CPU memory, ~100 GB uncompressed / 36 GB after FAISS compression [rag App. C, lines 1300-1304]. FAISS + Hierarchical Navigable Small World for approximate search [rag Sec.3, lines 283-284; ref 37].
state_decomposition.E_is_shared_and_read_only: E is global, corpus-level, and identical for every user and every query. There is no per-session or per-user state anywhere in the paper. Consequence for the chapter: RAG's C_cap is per-corpus, not per-session - the opposite of every later E-path paper.

equations.gloss: The read equation (R) with W = empty set. RAG is (R) minus the fast-weight slot.
equations.paper_form: p(y|x) with x the input and z ~ p_eta(.|x) the retrieved documents

equations.gloss: The retrieval operator of the unified frame, instantiated as a DPR bi-encoder inner product, resolved by Maximum Inner Product Search. phi_d is frozen; phi_q is part of Theta.
equations.paper_form: p_eta(z|x) proportional to exp( d(z)^T q(x) ),  d(z) = BERT_d(z),  q(x) = BERT_q(x)

equations.unified: \hat y \;=\; \arg\max_y \sum_{e\,\in\,\mathrm{ret}(E,q)} p(e\mid q)\prod_{i=1}^{N} p_\Theta\big(y_i \mid q, e, y_{1:i-1}\big)
equations.gloss: RAG-Sequence. One document is held responsible for the whole answer; marginalization happens once, outside the token product.
equations.paper_form: p_RAG-Sequence(y|x) approx sum_{z in top-k} p_eta(z|x) prod_i p_theta(y_i|x,z,y_{1:i-1})

equations.unified: \hat y \;=\; \arg\max_y \prod_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{e\,\in\,\mathrm{ret}(E,q)} p(e\mid q)\, p_\Theta\big(y_i \mid q, e, y_{1:i-1}\big)
equations.gloss: RAG-Token. Marginalization is inside the token product, so a different element of E may be responsible for each token. This is what lets one answer splice facts from several records; Figure 2 is the evidence.
equations.paper_form: p_RAG-Token(y|x) approx prod_i sum_{z in top-k} p_eta(z|x) p_theta(y_i|x,z,y_{1:i-1})

equations.gloss: Ordinary supervised fine-tuning with Adam. IMPORTANT: this has the SHAPE of (U-Theta) but not its content - the training set D is a fixed human-labelled corpus of (x_j, y_j) pairs, NOT gen(H_k; B_s). There is one such round (k = 0 -> 1), performed before deployment. No sleep round exists.
equations.paper_form: minimize sum_j -log p(y_j|x_j) with stochastic gradient descent using Adam [28]

equations.unified: p'_\Theta(y_i \mid q, y_{1:i-1}) \;=\; \sum_{e\,\in\,\mathrm{ret}(E,q)} p(e\mid q)\, p_\Theta(y_i \mid q, e, y_{1:i-1})
equations.gloss: RAG-Token decoding: the marginalized transition probability is plugged straight into a standard beam decoder. This is the cheap decode path.
equations.paper_form: p'_theta(y_i|x,y_{1:i-1}) = sum_{z in top-k} p_eta(z_i|x) p_theta(y_i|x,z_i,y_{1:i-1})

equations.unified: Y = \bigcup_{e \in \mathrm{ret}(E,q)} \mathrm{beam}(q,e), \qquad p(y\mid q) = \sum_{e} p(e\mid q)\, p_\Theta(y\mid q,e) \ \ \text{with an extra forward pass wherever } y \notin \mathrm{beam}(q,e)
equations.gloss: RAG-Sequence 'Thorough Decoding'. The expensive decode path: one beam search per retrieved element PLUS one extra forward pass per (hypothesis, element) pair missing from that element's beam. 'Fast Decoding' sets p_Theta(y|q,e) = 0 for those pairs instead, buying back the passes.

equations.unified: E_{k+1} \;=\; \mathrm{wr}(E_k,\ \hat c_k) \quad\text{with}\quad \hat c_k = c_k \ \ \text{(identity)},\ \ B_s = 0 \ \text{per context}
equations.gloss: The degenerate (U-E). What is written into E is the raw 100-word text chunk itself, embedded once by a frozen encoder. No offline inference S(c; B_s) is performed over the context before it is stored. The write is executed by the corpus pipeline, not by the model, and only ever as a wholesale index replacement (index hot-swapping). THIS DEGENERACY IS THE CHAPTER'S POINT: everything the later E-path adds is content for c-hat and an agent for wr.

outer_vs_inner.headline_for_the_reader: Nothing in RAG learns at test time. Every learnable object is fixed before the first query arrives. At wake time exactly one thing moves, and it is not a parameter: the identity of the K documents pulled out of E. If you have never trained a model, the honest one-line summary is: RAG is a normal fine-tuned model whose prompt is assembled by a lookup that was itself tuned during that same fine-tuning run.

update_layer.layers_touched_in_order: 1) Offline, once per corpus snapshot: build E by encoding 21M chunks with a frozen BERT_d and indexing with FAISS/HNSW - this is (U-E) with c-hat = identity and no model agency. 2) Offline, once: a (U-Theta)-shaped supervised fine-tuning round that moves Theta_gen and Theta_q jointly through the marginalization, with E held fixed. 3) At wake, per query: ret(E,q) only - equation (R) with W = empty set. No layer is written at wake time. 4) On world change: replace E wholesale; Theta untouched, no retraining [rag Sec.4.5].
update_layer.the_gap_this_leaves: Model-authored wr(E, c-hat) with a non-trivial c-hat is exactly the hole MemGPT and Letta STC fill. State this in the E-path bridge-out: RAG hands the next chapter a store that only humans can write to, containing only text that was already written.

cost_table.preamble: Rule applied strictly: only quantities the paper itself states. The paper reports no wall-clock, no throughput, no FLOPs, and no latency anywhere. Its cost reporting is entirely in bytes and parameter counts. A missing number here is a finding, not an omission of this note.

what_is_stated_instead: Training hardware: 'distributing training across 8, 32GB NVIDIA V100 GPUs, though training and inference can be run on one GPU', mixed precision, Fairseq [rag App. C, lines 1297-1299]. No GPU-hours, no step count, no epoch count.

Index construction: 'We use the document encoder to compute an embedding for each document, and build a single MIPS index using FAISS ... with a Hierarchical Navigable Small World approximation' over 21M documents [rag Sec.3, lines 280-284]. No time, no cost, no FLOPs given for this pass.

The paper explicitly names index maintenance as the cost it is avoiding: 'Updating the document encoder BERT_d during training is costly as it requires the document index to be periodically updated as REALM does during pre-training' [rag Sec.2.4, lines 252-253]. Costly is asserted, never quantified.
B_s.note_writer_reading: In the sleep-time frame the per-context B_s is zero by construction: no offline inference is performed over a context before storage. The only offline compute is a corpus-level, one-time encoding of 21M chunks, amortized over every query the deployment ever serves. Do not report this as a B_s number - the paper gives none.

what_is_stated_instead: Retrieval is claimed sub-linear but never timed: MIPS 'can be approximately solved in sub-linear time [23]' [rag Sec.2.2, lines 227-228].

'We find that doing Maximum Inner Product Search with FAISS is sufficiently fast on CPU, so we store document index vectors on CPU' [rag App. C, lines 1299-1300]. 'Sufficiently fast' is the paper's entire latency statement.

Wake-time work is described structurally in Sec.2.5: RAG-Token plugs a marginalized transition into a standard beam decoder; RAG-Sequence Thorough Decoding runs 'beam search for each document z' and then 'an additional forward pass for each document z for which y does not appear in the beam'. 'For longer output sequences, |Y| can become large, requiring many forward passes' [rag Sec.2.5, lines 264-273]. Fast Decoding removes those extra passes by approximation.

Test-time fan-out, which sets the decode multiplier: 15 retrieved documents for RAG-Token and 50 for RAG-Sequence on open-domain QA; 10 for both on Open-MSMarco and Jeopardy; beam size 4 for the generation tasks, greedy decoding for QA [rag App. A, lines 1273-1279].

The paper acknowledges the runtime axis exists and then declines to plot it: retrieving more documents at test time 'can affect performance and runtime' [rag Sec.4.5, line 799] - Figure 3 sweeps K from 10 to 50 on three quality axes and on none of runtime.
L_w.note_writer_reading: L_w is unreported but structurally large: the generator's prefill is over K concatenated (query, 100-word passage) contexts, K up to 50, plus a CPU-side ANN search off the GPU critical path. The chapter must say 'the paper reports no latency' and then reason about the shape only.

amortization_N_q.detail: The paper never writes an amortization argument and never reports how many queries share a retrieved context. amortization_N_q.why_it_does_not_apply: Equation (A) needs a per-context sleep cost to divide by N_q. RAG has none: the offline cost is per-corpus and effectively amortized over the entire deployment lifetime, so N_q* is unbounded and the break-even question is vacuous. This is the structural reason RAG is cheap and the reason the later E-path, which pays per-context, has to argue amortization at all. Say so explicitly in the chapter.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The expensive decode path's cost is described only qualitatively. Thorough Decoding runs a beam search per retrieved document and then 'an additional forward pass for each document z for which y does not appear in the beam', and 'For longer output sequences, |Y| can become large, requiring many forward passes'. The knowledge-staleness result rests on an 82-item, template-generated, author-built probe ('Who is {position}?' over world leaders whose office changed), and even with a matched index accuracy is only 70% and 68%.

Everything is measured on a single corpus: one December 2018 Wikipedia dump (plus a December 2016 dump used solely for the hot-swap probe). No noisy web corpus, no domain corpus, no multi-corpus mixing, no private or per-user partition is tested - despite the Broader Impact section proposing exactly that use ('by endowing it with a medical index').

grounded_in_paper.claim: The generator's prefill is multiplied by the retrieval fan-out. Each of the K retrieved passages is simply concatenated with the input ('To combine the input x with the retrieved content z when generating from BART, we simply concatenate them'), and K at test time is 15 for RAG-Token and 50 for RAG-Sequence on open-domain QA, 10 for the generation tasks.
grounded_in_paper.reader_translation: K=50 means fifty independent (question + 100-word passage) contexts through a 400M encoder-decoder per query. Passages are 100 words each [rag Sec.3], so the added prompt mass is bounded and small per passage but linear in K.

grounded_in_paper.claim: The two model variants have structurally different decode costs. RAG-Token's marginalized transition plugs into one standard beam decoder; RAG-Sequence needs one beam search per document plus extra forward passes for hypotheses absent from a document's beam.
grounded_in_paper.reader_translation: RAG-Token = one decode loop with a K-way mixture at each step. RAG-Sequence Thorough = K decode loops plus up to |Y| x K rescoring forwards. The paper adopts Fast Decoding for the long-output tasks precisely to avoid the second term.

grounded_in_paper.claim: The store lives in CPU DRAM, not on the accelerator: ~100 GB uncompressed, 36 GB compressed with FAISS, 21M x 728 values storable at 8 bits.
grounded_in_paper.source: [rag App. C, lines 1299-1304; App. G, lines 1427-1429]
grounded_in_paper.reader_translation: This is a host-memory-resident, read-mostly structure sitting outside HBM, searched by an HNSW graph walk on CPU while the GPU holds a 400M-parameter model. In the memory hierarchy, E is DRAM/NVMe territory and Theta is HBM territory - and RAG is the paper that first pins them to different devices.

grounded_in_paper.claim: Search is claimed sub-linear and 'sufficiently fast on CPU', which is why the vectors were placed there in the first place.
grounded_in_paper.reader_translation: The design decision is stated; the latency it implies is not. Take the placement as fact and the speed as an unquantified author judgement.

grounded_in_paper.claim: Updating world knowledge costs an index rebuild and no gradient step: 'we can update RAG's world knowledge by simply replacing its non-parametric memory', measured as 68% correct on the fresh index versus 4% on the two-year-stale one.
grounded_in_paper.reader_translation: In the reader's vocabulary: the deployment artefact does not change. No checkpoint is rewritten, no serving weights are swapped, no per-user delta appears. Contrast the Theta-path, where a knowledge update is a redeploy.

grounded_in_paper.claim: K is a test-time dial: 'We have the flexibility to adjust the number of retrieved documents at test time, which can affect performance and runtime.'
grounded_in_paper.reader_translation: A quality/cost knob that requires no retraining - and, per Figure 3, one whose quality return is monotone for RAG-Sequence and non-monotone for RAG-Token (peak at 10). An operator can trade SLA for accuracy per request.

grounded_in_paper.claim: Training fits on 8 x 32GB V100 with mixed precision, and 'training and inference can be run on one GPU'.

The index is built once with a frozen encoder specifically to avoid the periodic re-embedding REALM requires: 'Updating the document encoder BERT_d during training is costly as it requires the document index to be periodically updated'.
grounded_in_paper.reader_translation: The paper's one explicit systems trade: freeze the document tower, accept a slightly stale embedding function, and buy a static index. It reports no measurement of the accuracy given up.

note_writer_inferences.inference: Shared-weight batching survives intact. E is global and read-only and Theta is fixed after fine-tuning, so every request in a batch uses the same weights and the same index; only the retrieved passages differ, and those enter as prompt tokens. This is the property the Theta-path loses the moment per-user weight deltas appear (STC-STYLE Sec.3 Rosetta row 'batch로 weight 공유').
note_writer_inferences.grounding: Inference from the architecture as described [rag Sec.2, Sec.2.4]; the paper never discusses batching.

note_writer_inferences.inference: Batching is nonetheless perturbed in a different way: the effective sequence count per request is K, not 1, so a batch of B requests is B x K generator contexts. Continuous-batching schedulers see a request whose token cost is set by a retrieval hyperparameter rather than by the user's prompt.
note_writer_inferences.grounding: Inference from Sec.2.3's concatenation and App. A's K values; no throughput number in the paper.

note_writer_inferences.inference: There is a CPU-GPU round trip on the critical path of every query: embed the query on GPU (or CPU), search HNSW on CPU, ship K passages back, then prefill. TTFT therefore contains a host-side ANN traversal that scales with index size, not with prompt length.
note_writer_inferences.grounding: Placement is stated [rag App. C]; the round trip and its latency consequence are the note writer's inference. The paper measures neither.

note_writer_inferences.inference: The bytes moved per query are dominated by index traffic, not by model weights: an HNSW walk touches a data-dependent set of 728-dimensional vectors scattered across tens of gigabytes of DRAM, which is a random-access, low-arithmetic-intensity workload - the opposite of the dense GEMMs the reader is used to. This is the E-path's characteristic memory signature and the reason retrieval sits on CPU here at all.
note_writer_inferences.grounding: Inference. The paper gives the vector count, dimensionality, and footprint [rag App. G, App. C] but no access counts and no bandwidth measurement.

note_writer_inferences.inference: Because per-context sleep cost is zero and the index is amortized across the whole deployment, RAG's cost model has no break-even point to compute. Equation (A) degenerates: C_avg = C_wake, with C_wake inflated by the factor K. The E-path's later papers move cost from the amortized corpus-level term into a per-context term, and that is precisely when amortization arguments become necessary.
note_writer_inferences.grounding: Inference from the unified frame applied to the paper's mechanism; the paper contains no amortization discussion.

systems_implications.the_readers_question: So what does it change at decode? Three things, and only three. (1) Prefill mass is multiplied by K - up to 50 concatenated passage contexts per query [App. A], with no latency number attached. (2) A host-side approximate-nearest-neighbour search over 36-100 GB of DRAM enters the critical path before the first token [App. C]. (3) Nothing about the deployment artefact changes when knowledge changes - the fix is to rebuild an index, not to retrain or redeploy [Sec.4.5]. Everything else the reader knows about serving still holds: weights are shared, batching is unbroken, no per-user state exists.
